facts.text: No study defines a false alarm rate that operators of off-road machines will accept.
facts.quote: No study defines a false alarm rate that operators of off-road machines will accept.

facts.text: The ACARP project explicitly listed an "acceptable false alarm rate" among questions requiring further research.
facts.quote: The ACARP project explicitly listed "acceptable false alarm rate" among the questions still requiring further research [15].

facts.text: An 18% false-alarm rate caused problems in the 2006 field test.
facts.quote: An 18% false-alarm rate caused problems in the 2006 field test

facts.text: The problems associated with an 18% false-alarm rate in the 2006 field test do not establish that 17% or 5% would be acceptable; nuisance rate, urgency, alarm modality, operating phase and consequence all matter.
facts.quote: but it does not follow that 17% is acceptable or that 5% would be: nuisance rate, urgency, alarm modality, operating phase and consequence all matter [3].

facts.text: Studies summarized in Accident Analysis & Prevention in 2023 linked an 18% false alarm rate to underuse of forward collision warning (FCW) in road trucks.
facts.quote: A false alarm rate of 18% was linked to underuse of FCW in trucks;

facts.text: In road-truck FCW studies summarized in Accident Analysis & Prevention in 2023, drivers ignored warnings (12%) or stopped using the system (11%).
facts.quote: drivers ignored warnings (12%) or stopped using the system (11%) (studies summarized in Accident Analysis & Prevention, 2023) [16].

facts.text: Lees and Lee (2007) found that warnings with more than 20% false alarms can still shorten brake reaction times in driving simulators.
facts.quote: Warnings with more than 20% false alarms can still shorten brake reaction times (Lees and Lee, 2007) [17].

facts.text: A 2025 driving-simulator study found that 33% false alarms did not produce a "cry wolf" effect.
facts.quote: A 2025 simulator study found that 33% false alarms did not produce a "cry wolf" effect

facts.text: A 2025 driving-simulator study found that 33% false alarms caused unnecessary braking.
facts.quote: A 2025 simulator study found that 33% false alarms did not produce a "cry wolf" effect but did cause unnecessary braking [18].

facts.text: Wickens et al. (2009) reported that 45% of air traffic control conflict alerts were false, with no evidence of cry-wolf behavior; this evidence concerns air traffic control, not driving.
facts.quote: *Air traffic control (not driving).* 45% of conflict alerts were false, with no evidence of cry-wolf behavior (Wickens et al., 2009) [75].

facts.text: In naturalistic FCW evidence from the USA associated with NHTSA/Leidos, false alerts were 12% when turning versus 2% during lane-keeping.
facts.quote: *Naturalistic FCW (USA, NHTSA/Leidos).* False alerts were 12% when turning against 2% in lane-keeping

facts.text: In naturalistic FCW evidence from the USA associated with NHTSA/Leidos, drivers turned alert sensitivity down over time.
facts.quote: and drivers turned alert sensitivity down over time [76].

facts.text: On-road evidence from Lees and Lee (2007) and a 2026 study of timing errors and false alarms in road-hazard detection indicates that unnecessary alarms with a plausible cause hurt trust less than alarms with no visible cause.
facts.quote: Unnecessary alarms with a plausible cause hurt trust less than alarms with no visible cause (Lees and Lee, 2007; a 2026 study of timing errors and false alarms in road-hazard detection) [17, 77].

facts.text: For operator acceptance and automatic braking, false positives per detection alone are unlikely to be the useful metric; this is an expert synthesis, not a published standard.
facts.quote: A design implication follows: the useful metric is unlikely to be false positives per detection alone.

facts.text: For operator acceptance and automatic braking, task-stratified unnecessary warnings or interventions per operating hour, loading cycle, reverse manoeuvre and legitimate close approach are more informative metrics. This recommendation is a synthesis from the evidence, not a published standard.
facts.quote: For operator acceptance and for automatic braking, unnecessary warnings or interventions per operating hour, per loading cycle, per reverse manoeuvre and per legitimate close approach, stratified by task, are more informative.
